# Framework Security Boundaries

Dimension covering how agent frameworks implement (or fail to implement)
security boundaries between agents and tools. See [citations.md](../citations.md)
for source details.

## Framework Security Matrix

| Framework | Tool Scoping | Code Sandbox | HITL Approval | Auth/AuthZ | CVEs (2025-2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI Agents SDK | Per-agent tools | No native | needsApproval | API key | — |
| Microsoft Semantic Kernel | Filters | No native | Via filters | Azure RBAC | — |
| Google ADK | Callbacks + plugins | Vertex sandbox | Via callbacks | OAuth | — |

## Enforced vs. Advisory Controls

The fundamental distinction in framework security: most "guardrails" are
advisory (probabilistic prompt-based guidance) rather than enforced
(deterministic code-level boundaries).

**Advisory controls:** The model follows them because the response is
statistically likely given the system prompt — not because enforcement
prevents violation.

**Enforced controls:** Code-level mechanisms the LLM cannot bypass through
prompt manipulation. Examples: Semantic Kernel filters [26], SEAgent ABAC
policies [4], CaMeL capability tokens [15], sandbox kernel boundaries.

## Per-Framework Analysis

### OpenAI Agents SDK

- Guardrails as first-class concepts with optimistic execution [46]
- Input guardrails on user's initial input, output guardrails on final response
- Runs validation in parallel with agent execution (fail-fast) [46]
- `needsApproval` parameter on tools for HITL [46]
- No native sandbox for code execution
- Instruction hierarchy (System > Developer > User > Tool) trained into
  model [33]

### Microsoft Semantic Kernel

- Zero trust approach: treats all inserted content as unsafe by default [26]
- HTML encoding prevents prompt injection by encoding unsafe content during
  prompt rendering [26]
- Three deterministic filter types run at key execution points [26]:
  - Function Invocation Filter (before/after every function call)
  - Prompt Render Filter (before prompt submission)
  - Auto Function Invocation Filter (during automatic calling)
- Filters can block execution, override results, retry with alternatives [26]
- Integration path to Azure Prompt Shields via filters [25]
- `allow_dangerously_set_content` parameter defaults to false [26]

### Google ADK

- Three safety dimensions: identity/authorization, input/output screening,
  execution isolation [27]
- OAuth-based identity: agents only access what the controlling user can [27]
- Before/after tool callbacks for pre-validation [27]
- Plugin architecture: Gemini as Judge, Model Armor, PII Redaction [27]
- Code Executor tool integrates with Vertex Code Interpreter Extension for
  sandboxed execution [27]
- VPC-SC perimeter integration [27]
- Recommends hermetic execution environments with no network connections [27]

### LangGraph / LangChain

- Authentication via `@auth.authenticate` handlers, authorization via
  `@auth.on` handlers for per-resource validation
- LangChain deprecated native sandbox (Pyodide+Deno) — no longer recommended
  for production
- LangSmith Sandboxes (private preview): microVM isolation with
  authentication proxy keeping secrets outside runtime
- SOC 2 Type II / HIPAA / GDPR compliance for LangSmith platform
- 57.3% of organizations have agents in production (survey)

**CVEs (March 2026):**
- CVE-2026-34070: Path traversal (CVSS 7.5)
- CVE-2025-67644: SQL injection (CVSS 7.3)
- CVE-2025-68664: Deserialization / secret exfiltration (CVSS 9.3)

### CrewAI

- Task-level guardrails with LLM judges and code validation
- Automatic retry up to 2× on guardrail failure
- Sequential and hierarchical process types
- Partnership with NemoClaw for infrastructure-level enforcement

**CVEs (March 2026):**
- CVE-2026-2275: Arbitrary C function calls via ctypes when Docker unreachable
- CVE-2026-2287, CVE-2026-2285, CVE-2026-2286: Additional sandbox escape
  vulnerabilities
- Child agents inherit parent's full credentials with no scope narrowing

### AutoGen

- Docker container code execution with sandboxed Python runner
- File system access and network call restrictions
- **AutoGen Studio explicitly "not meant for production"** — lacks security
  features
- Microsoft Agent Framework integration provides Azure RBAC, VNet, private
  endpoints

## Sandbox Technologies

| Technology | Isolation Level | Used By |
|---|---|---|
| Firecracker microVMs | Strongest (separate kernel) | LangSmith Sandboxes |
| gVisor | User-space kernel interception | GKE Agent Sandbox |
| Docker containers | Shared host kernel | AutoGen, CrewAI |
| Landlock LSM + seccomp | Process-level | NemoClaw |
| No sandbox | None | Most production deployments |

Docker Sandboxes (Desktop 4.60+) evolved from containers to dedicated
microVMs, acknowledging container isolation is insufficient for untrusted
agent-generated code.

## Credential Delegation Problem

In multi-agent systems, child agents inherit parent's full credentials with
no scope narrowing or depth limits [44]. This creates cascading confused
deputy risk at every delegation hop.

93% of audited AI agent projects use unscoped API keys with no enforcement
of scope narrowing or cascade revocation (from industry audit report).

## Gaps and Limitations

- Framework security features are opt-in — most default to permissive
- No framework provides end-to-end enforced security boundaries across
  the full agent-tool-agent chain
- CVE clustering in March 2026 (LangChain + CrewAI) suggests systematic
  rather than isolated security issues
- Credential delegation in multi-agent systems has no standardized solution
- Performance cost of enforced vs advisory controls not benchmarked
- Regulatory compliance gap: EU AI Act enforcement deadline August 2, 2026
  with €35M fines, but framework compliance tools immature
